posts.title: 子供へのチャットGPTの使わせ方を考える
posts.content:
> AIは正解の回答を出したはずなのに全員を不幸にした
何とは言いませんが、あるニュースを見て、かなり考えさせられました。（その件については触れません。）
一視聴者としてもいろいろ感じることはあったのですが、
AIに関わる立場として特に思ったのは、
「子どもにチャットGPTをどう使わせるべきか」ということです。
うちには4人の子どもがいます。
一番上の息子は小学2年生ですが、iPhoneやiPadは普通に使えるし、パソコンもある程度触れます。タイピングも少しできるし、国語が得意で、今は小学4年生向けの漢字や国語の教材を自分から進めています。
つまり、AIを使おうと思えば使えると思います。少なからず今後5年間のうちにチャットGPTを使い始めるだろうと思ってます。
とはいえ、子どもにチャットGPTを積極的に使わせたいかと聞かれると、正直なところ、まだ慎重に考えたいというのが本音です。
でも時代の流れを見れば、AIを使うことは当たり前になっていくのでしょう。
そこで、これから子どもたちにチャットGPTをどう使わせていくべきか、自分なりの考えを整理しておきたいと思います。
チャットGPTは、答えを知るには便利。
漢字の読み方を調べる、計算の考え方を学ぶ、歴史の出来事を確認する、目の前にあるパソコンがどう作られているのかを調べる。こういう「知りたいことを調べる道具」としては、かなり使えると思っています。
一方で、抽象的な相談や、日常のモヤモヤをそのままAIに投げる使い方は、子どもには危ういとも感じてます。
AIが答えたから。

調べたらそう書いてあったから。

チャットGPTがこう言ったから。
そうやって、判断までAIに預けてしまうのは怖い。
答えを出すことと、実際に行動することは別です。
行動することはメリットを及ぼします。
その反面で行動には責任が伴います。その結果をAIが知ることはできません。
AIは流石に未来は分からないのです。人に聞いてもAIに聞いてもその後の展開は分かりません。
そう整理すると、見えてくるのは
分からないことの判断を、AIにも人にも委ねてはならない。
これは大人でも同じですよね。
AIに聞いて、理解してない答えをそのまま仕事に使うのは、仕事ができない人の典型ではないですか。
僕自身は、AIには「相談相手」というより決められたルールをこなす「作業者」として使うことが多いです。
整理する。

コピペする。

編集する。

資料を作る。

コードを書く。
こういう明確な作業には便利さを感じます。そこにはAIが判断する箇所を極力少なくしてるから。
でも、答えが四方八方に広がる抽象的な問いをチャットGPTに投げた場合、大人でも判断に困るような回答が返ってくることがあるし、常人には理解し難い回答を出すこともあり、実用的では無いと感じています。
それと、そもそも生成AIの文章生成は確率計算が基本で、そこにWeb検索やパーソナライズといった補完要素が組み合わさって回答が作られる仕組み。情などは無く、淡々ともっともな回答を出してるだけ。
それを、子どもがそのまま信じてしまう、理解した気になってしまうのは危険だと思います。
だから、子どもにチャットGPTを使わせるなら、いきなり自由に使わせるのではなく、用途を絞った小さなAIを用意するのが良さそう。
というのが、今回の件で思った、一旦の最適解です。
たとえば、国語の調べ物専用のAI。

計算の考え方を教える専用のAI。

歴史や理科の疑問に答える専用のAI。
何でも答える万能AIではなく、目的ごとに分けた小さなアプリのように使わせる。これが現実的かなと思っています。
もちろん、チャットGPTには保護者が管理する制限機能もあります。そういう機能も使いながら、親が使い方を見ていく必要があると思います。
そして、たぶん僕は子どもにこう伝えていきます。
「AIは使っても良い。でも、やり取りは全部見れるからね」

「AIが変な勘違いをしていたら、ちゃんと指摘するからね」

「AIの答えをそのまま信じるんじゃなくて、最後は自分で考えようね」
そして「なぜ、それが正しいと思ったの？」と問い詰める。
AIを使わせない、という選択肢はもう難しいと思ってます。
でも、何でも自由に使わせるのも、まだ違う。
大事なのは、AIを「神様」にしないこと。
あくまで、調べるための道具、学ぶための道具、作業を助ける道具として使わせること。
子どもにチャットGPTを使わせるなら、最初に教えるべきなのはプロンプトの書き方ではなく、
「AIの答えをどう受け取るか」なのかもしれません。
最後に、私の意見が全て正しいとは思っていません。皆さんの考えも伺ったうえで、自分の中で改めて整理したいと考えています。コメントや引用などでご意見をいただけると嬉しいです。

【衝撃】
Claude Codeを作った本人（Boris）が
 「俺、毎晩寝てる間に数千のClaude Code動かしてる」
と57分の動画で全部バラしてる動画が話題😳 https://t.co/6Fb63UcQcY
夜中、本人はスマホで通知見てるだけ。 数千体のAIが、勝手に仕事を片付けていく。これ普通の人と比べると、差がエグい👇

❌ タブを6個開いて、ターミナルで1個ずつ手で世話する
→これでも上級者
⭕ 数千体に同時に走らせて、人は通知を眺めるだけ
→流石Claude Codeの生みの親

同じClaude Codeなのに、出力が桁違い。 なんでこんな芸当ができるのか整理👇

・夜のうちにタスクを振って、寝てる間に走らせる
・1体ずつ会話せず、何千体を一気に並列起動
・各エージェントの進捗はスマホ通知でチェック
・朝、出来上がった成果物だけまとめてレビュー
・人間がやるのは「最後にOKを出す」判断だけ

要は、AIを“1人のアシスタント”じゃなく “チーム”として扱ってる。

「並列で大量に回す」 これがClaude Codeの本当の伸びしろ。

作った本人が、一番ぶっ飛んだ使い方をしてる件。

このチーム化、本人の運用Tipsにそのまま落ちてる。

Boris本人が実践する最強Tips30選、 読むと使い方が一段変わるからおすすめ👇

posts.content:
The most dangerous thing happening in software right now?

AI coding agents are quietly changing what it means to be a developer.

Not in 10 years.

Right now.

Claude Code and Codex are pushing two completely different futures:

Claude Code:
“Keep the engineer in the loop.”

Codex:
“Remove the loop.”

One optimizes for deep reasoning.
The other optimizes for autonomous execution.

And honestly?

This is the first real split in AI-native software engineering.

You can already feel it inside engineering teams:

Some developers want an AI that thinks carefully beside them.

Others want an AI army shipping PRs while they sleep.

That’s not a tooling difference.

That’s a philosophical divide.

The wild part is that both sides are right.

Because the future developer probably doesn’t look like a programmer anymore.

They look more like:
• an architect
• a systems orchestrator
• an operator of autonomous agents

We spent years arguing about “AI replacing developers.”

Wrong debate.

AI is replacing parts of the software workflow itself.

And the companies that understand this early are going to move terrifyingly fast.

posts.title: Agentic Programming Is the New Full-Stack Development
posts.content:
Most people still think AI agents are “ChatGPT with tools.”

That’s not what’s happening anymore.

We are entering a completely different era of software engineering — one where applications don’t just respond to inputs, but actively reason, plan, execute workflows, recover from failures, and operate toward goals autonomously.

And the crazy part?

Most developers are still learning prompts while the industry is quietly shifting toward agentic systems.

The companies building the next generation of software are no longer asking:

“How do we integrate AI?”

They’re asking:

“How do we build systems where AI becomes the operating layer?”

That’s the difference between AI features and agentic architecture.

This article is a complete roadmap to understanding agentic programming from scratch:

- what it actually is
- how agents work internally
- the architecture behind production systems
- memory and tool design
- frameworks worth learning
- common failure modes
- how to build your first production-ready agent
- and the exact roadmap I’d follow if I had to start again today

If you deeply understand the concepts in this article, you’ll already be ahead of most developers entering AI today.

What Is Agentic Programming?

Traditional software follows deterministic logic.

Input → code → output.

Agentic systems work differently.

They receive a goal, reason about possible actions, use tools, observe outcomes, adapt their strategy, and continue iterating until the task is complete.

A chatbot generates responses.

An agent generates outcomes.

That distinction changes everything.

A real agent can:

- research competitors
- write reports
- debug code
- browse websites
- call APIs
- update databases
- automate workflows
- coordinate multiple agents
- recover from failures
- ask for clarification when needed

The model is no longer just a text generator.

It becomes the decision-making engine inside a larger software system.

“The future of software is not apps with AI.
It’s AI operating the apps.”

The Biggest Misconception About AI Agents

Most beginners think building agents is mostly prompting.

It’s not.

Prompting matters, but production agents are primarily a systems engineering problem.

The hard parts are:

- memory architecture
- state management
- tool orchestration
- observability
- retry handling
- cost optimization
- context management
- failure recovery
- permissions and guardrails

This is why so many demos look impressive but collapse in real-world environments.

A prompt can create a cool demo.

Architecture creates reliable systems.

The Foundations You Must Learn First

Before touching frameworks like LangGraph or CrewAI, learn the actual foundations.

This step is non-negotiable.

1. Python

Almost the entire AI ecosystem is Python-first.

You need to become comfortable with:

- functions
- classes
- async/await
- APIs
- file systems
- JSON
- exception handling
- HTTP requests
- queues and retries

Because most production agent systems are orchestration layers written in Python.

Here’s a simple example of calling an LLM API:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()

response = client.chat.completions.create(
model="gpt-4.1",
messages=[
{"role": "user", "content": "Explain vector databases simply"}
]
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

Simple.

But real systems become much more complex once tools, memory, and multi-step reasoning enter the picture.

2. Understand How LLMs Actually Work

You do NOT need a PhD.

But you DO need to understand:

- tokenization
- context windows
- embeddings
- temperature
- sampling
- hallucinations
- retrieval
- structured outputs

For example:

If your context window becomes overloaded, your agent’s reasoning quality degrades significantly.

That’s why memory systems exist.

3. Learn Embeddings Early

This is one of the most important concepts in modern AI systems.

Embeddings transform text into vectors.

Those vectors allow semantic similarity search.

This powers:

- RAG systems
- long-term memory
- semantic retrieval
- recommendation engines
- contextual search

Without embeddings, your agents cannot retrieve relevant knowledge efficiently.

Here’s a simple embedding example:

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI()

embedding = client.embeddings.create(
model="text-embedding-3-small",
input="How do AI agents use memory?"
)

print(len(embedding.data[0].embedding))

That vector becomes searchable memory for your agents.

The Core Architecture Behind Every Agent

Almost every serious agent system contains four components.

1. Reasoning Engine

Usually the LLM.

It decides:

- what to do next
- which tool to call
- how to respond
- whether progress is being made

This is the “brain.”

2. Memory

Without memory, agents are stateless.

There are three important types:

Short-Term Memory

The active context window during the task.

Long-Term Memory

External retrieval systems like vector databases.

Episodic Memory

Records of previous runs, failures, and successful actions.

Production agents often combine all three.

“Memory is what transforms responses into behavior.”

3. Tools

Tools are how agents interact with the world.

Examples:

- web search
- browser automation
- APIs
- databases
- file writing
- code execution

The LLM reasons.

Tools execute.

Example tool definition:

tools = [
{
"name": "web_search",
"description": (
"Search the web for current information. "
"Use only when knowledge may be outdated."
),
"parameters": {
"query": {
"type": "string"
}
}
}
]

Good tool design dramatically improves reliability.

4. Goal Management

This is what separates workflows from conversations.

The agent decomposes large objectives into smaller subtasks.

Example:

- research topic
- collect sources
- summarize findings
- write report
- verify output

This decomposition is critical for complex systems.

The ReAct Loop: The Heart of Modern Agents

Most modern agents operate using the ReAct pattern.

Reason → Act → Observe → Repeat

This iterative loop is the foundation of agentic behavior.

Example:

Goal:
“Research top vector databases.”

Loop:

1. Search current vector databases
2. Compare pricing
3. Analyze performance
4. Gather documentation
5. Write report
6. Save file

The agent continuously updates its reasoning based on observations.

That iterative behavior is what makes agents powerful.

Building Your First Real Agent

Let’s build a minimal research agent.

This example demonstrates:

- tool calling
- reasoning loops
- memory accumulation
- execution flow

from openai import OpenAI
import requests

client = OpenAI()

def web_search(query):
return f"Search results for: {query}"

def run_agent(goal):

messages = [
    {
        "role": "system",
        "content": (
            "You are a research agent. "
            "Use tools when necessary."
        )
    },
    {
        "role": "user",
        "content": goal
    }
]

for step in range(5):

    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4.1",
        messages=messages
    )

    output = response.choices[0].message.content

    print(f"Step {step+1}:")
    print(output)

    messages.append({
        "role": "assistant",
        "content": output
    })

run_agent(
"Research the top vector databases in 2026"
)

This is obviously simplified.

But this structure evolves into production architectures surprisingly quickly.

Why Most AI Agents Fail in Production

This is where things become interesting.

Most failures are NOT model failures.

They are architecture failures.

Common Failure Modes

1. Infinite Loops

Agents repeatedly retry tasks without making progress.

2. Context Overflow

Too much information degrades reasoning quality.

3. Poor Tool Design

Ambiguous tools create hallucinated actions.

4. No Observability

Teams cannot debug what the agent actually did.

5. Weak Guardrails

Agents perform unintended actions.

6. Cost Explosion

Multi-step reasoning burns massive token volume.

These problems become very real at scale.

Observability Is Mandatory

If you cannot trace:

- prompts
- tool calls
- failures
- retries
- token usage

then you cannot debug production agents.

This is why tools like:

- LangSmith
- Helicone
- AgentOps

have become essential infrastructure.

Production agent engineering is increasingly about visibility.

Multi-Agent Systems

Single agents are useful.

Multi-agent systems are where things become extremely powerful.

Instead of one generalist agent, you create specialists.

Example:

- Researcher Agent
- Writer Agent
- Reviewer Agent
- Planner Agent

Each handles one responsibility.

This improves:

- scalability
- reliability
- modularity
- debugging
- specialization

Example architecture:

agents = {
"researcher": "Find information",
"writer": "Write content",
"reviewer": "Validate quality"
}

workflow = [
"researcher",
"writer",
"reviewer"
]

This mirrors how real organizations operate.

The Frameworks Worth Learning

The framework ecosystem is stabilizing around a few major players.

LangGraph

Best for:

- production systems
- state management
- branching workflows
- observability
- long-running tasks

LangGraph treats workflows like graphs instead of chains.

This makes complex orchestration dramatically easier.

CrewAI

Best for:

- multi-agent collaboration
- fast prototyping
- role-based systems

Very intuitive for orchestrator-worker architectures.

Direct APIs

Sometimes the best framework is no framework.

Direct OpenAI or Anthropic APIs give:

- full flexibility
- zero abstraction
- maximum control

A lot of advanced teams eventually move closer to raw APIs.

The Most Important Production Principle

Human-in-the-loop systems are GOOD architecture.

Not weakness.

High-stakes systems should include approval checkpoints.

Especially for:

- financial actions
- external communication
- customer support
- database updates

The best AI systems augment humans.

They don’t blindly replace them.

The Real Skill Gap in AI

The market is flooded with people who can prompt models.

Far fewer can:

- design agent architectures
- manage memory systems
- orchestrate workflows
- debug failures
- optimize cost
- build reliable autonomous systems

That’s where the real opportunity is.

“The next generation of software engineers will architect behavior, not just code.”

A Realistic 6-Month Roadmap

Months 1–2

Focus:

- Python
- APIs
- LLM basics
- prompt engineering
- embeddings

Build:

- summarizers
- structured extractors
- simple tool-calling apps

Months 3–4

Focus:

- vector databases
- memory systems
- RAG
- ReAct loops
- deployment

Build:

- research agents
- retrieval systems
- autonomous workflows

Learn:

- LangGraph OR CrewAI

Not both initially.

Months 5–6

Focus:

- multi-agent systems
- observability
- evaluation
- production deployment

Build:

- orchestrator-worker systems
- specialized agent pipelines
- real-world automations

Deploy them publicly.

That changes everything.

Final Thoughts

We are extremely early.

Most companies still do not know how to deploy reliable agentic systems.

Most developers still underestimate how large this shift actually is.

But this transition is very real.

Software is evolving from:
“tools humans operate”
to
“systems that operate on behalf of humans.”

And the engineers who understand:

- reasoning systems
- memory architectures
- orchestration
- tool ecosystems
- autonomous workflows

will shape the next decade of technology.

The important thing is not learning endlessly.

It’s building.

Build messy systems.
Break them.
Debug them.
Ship them.
Improve them.

That feedback loop is where real expertise comes from.

Because eventually there’s a moment where it clicks:

You stop thinking of AI as a chatbot.

And start thinking of it as infrastructure.
